analysis.one_liner: Charges offshore oil and gas drillers $10 per acre to fund renewable energy research.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy Committee in May 2010, drew no cosponsors, and died there when Congress ended that January without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge oil and gas companies $10 per acre each year for the federal offshore waters they lease for drilling. The money would go into a new Treasury fund for researching and deploying renewable technologies that cut oil use and greenhouse gas emissions. It was introduced a month after the BP Deepwater Horizon spill and named after BP's "Beyond Petroleum" slogan, but it never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The public would gain a dedicated funding stream for technologies that reduce oil dependence and greenhouse gas emissions, funded entirely by offshore drillers rather than taxpayers [S2][S3]. Renewable energy researchers and companies would gain a new source of federal research, development, and deployment money, administered jointly by the EPA, Energy, and Transportation departments [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renewable energy research and the public

how_it_helps.text: Creates a dedicated 'Oil Dependence Reduction Fund' that can only be spent on renewable technologies or programs that significantly decrease oil use and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, with annual public reporting on every dollar deposited and spent.
Makes the oil industry pay for the transition: a $10-per-acre annual fee on leased federal offshore acreage feeds the fund, so ordinary taxpayers are not the ones funding oil-dependence research.
Includes an anti-evasion provision letting the Interior Secretary write rules to prevent companies from structuring leases to dodge the fee.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies holding federal offshore leases as of May 1, 2010 would pay $10 per acre per year [S2][S3]. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers at the gas pump, though $10 per acre is a small charge relative to the value of offshore production (general point about how fees on producers work).

drawbacks.text: The fee is small: $10 per acre per year would likely raise a modest amount of money relative to the scale of the oil-dependence and climate problem, so the bill is more of a signal than a transformation.
Money only flows to the fund if Congress actually appropriates it each year; fees are 'subject to appropriation,' so lawmakers could collect the fee and let the money sit unspent.
Fees on producers tend to be passed through to consumers in the form of somewhat higher fuel prices, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is modest and honestly structured: a small, hard-to-evade fee on offshore drillers, a fund legally barred from spending on anything but oil-reduction and emissions technology, and required annual public accounting. Its main weaknesses are scale and fragility — the revenue would be small, and the spending depends on annual appropriations. The costs are correspondingly small, though some could reach consumers at the pump.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Frank Lautenberg introduced the bill on May 11, 2010, about three weeks after the BP Deepwater Horizon rig explosion began the largest offshore oil spill in U.S. history.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies holding federal offshore leases are better off, because no fee was ever enacted; the Oil Dependence Reduction Fund was never created, so renewable energy programs received nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore drillers; the fee never became law

for.name: Sen. Frank Lautenberg
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in May 2010 and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only positional signal is that a Democrat sponsored the bill and no senator of either party cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill would impose a $10-per-acre annual fee on every leased federal offshore acre held as of May 1, 2010, with the proceeds going to oil-reduction research. The industry avoids the fee because the bill died in committee.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and clean technology firms
industries.note: A new dedicated fund would pay for research, development, deployment, and expansion of technologies that cut oil use and emissions. It was never funded.
